'''Aaron Lemonick''' (February 2, 1923 – June 19, 2003) was a [[Princeton University]] [[physics]] professor and administrator who served as dean of the graduate school from 1969 to 1973,<ref name="deans">{{Cite web |url=https://gradschool.princeton.edu/about/history |title=History |website=[[Princeton University Graduate School]] |access-date=2021-07-17}}</ref> and as dean of the faculty from 1973 to 1989. [[Joseph Hooton Taylor Jr.|Joseph Taylor]], winner of the 1993 [[Nobel Prize]] in Physics, attributes his decision to study physics instead of mathematics to Lemonick's freshman physics course at [[Haverford College|Haverford]].<ref name="Obituary">[https://www.princeton.edu/pr/news/03/q2/0620-lemonick.htm Aaron Lemonick, longtime faculty member and administrator, dies at age 80<!-- Bot generated title -->]</ref> Princeton awarded him the President's Award for Distinguished Teaching when he retired in 1994, and he received an honorary degree in 2001.<ref name="Obituary"/>

Lemonick served in the [[United States Air Force|US Air Force]] during World War II, and later attended the [[University of Pennsylvania]] as an undergraduate. He began his association with Princeton as a graduate student in physics and received his Ph.D. in 1954. He taught at Haverford College and became chair of the physics department there in 1957, as well as working as a research collaborator at [[Brookhaven National Laboratory]]. He became a member of the Princeton faculty as an associate professor of physics in 1961.<ref name="Obituary"/> He was elected a Fellow of the [[American Physical Society]] in 1964.<ref>{{cite web|title=APS Fellow Archive|url=https://www.aps.org/programs/honors/fellowships/archive-all.cfm?initial=&year=1964&unit_id=&institution=Princeton+University}}</ref> He was the father of Science writer [[Michael D. Lemonick]]<ref name="Moment">{{Cite web | url=http://www.princeton.edu/paw/archive_new/PAW03-04/10-0310/moment.html |title = PAW March 10, 2004: A moment with}}</ref>

[[Ruth Simmons]], the 18th president of Brown, who worked under Lemonick as a Princeton administrator, cites him as one of the major influences on her career.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Simmons |first=Ruth J. |date=2006-02-05 |title=Doing It Right Matters |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2006/02/05/business/yourmoney/doing-it-right-matters.html |access-date=2025-02-27 |work=The New York Times |language=en-US |issn=0362-4331}}</ref> He was also a force behind the foundation of Princeton's [[Women's Studies]] program,<ref>{{Cite news |date=1985-06-16 |title=PRINCETON FOSTERING WOMEN'S STUDIES |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1985/06/16/nyregion/princeton-fostering-women-s-studies.html |access-date=2025-02-27 |work=The New York Times |language=en-US |issn=0362-4331}}</ref> as well as its [[Molecular Biology]] department.
